newsitem.title: CONGO: Ex-leader defiant in Congo Brazzaville standoff.
newsitem.headline: Ex-leader defiant in Congo Brazzaville standoff.

text.p: The former military leader of Congo Brazzaville said on Friday that his supporters would resist any attempt by the government to use force to delay presidential elections planned for July 27.

Denis Sassou Nguesso told Radio France International one day after troops surrounded his home and fought gunbattles with his supporters that President Pascal Lissouba had to make clear whether he wanted peaceful elections.
"There is no doubt they (my supporters) will resist. We cannot accept that the (electoral) process be put in doubt by force," he said in an interview.
Officials say the government wants peaceful elections and accuse Sassou Nguesso of stirring up trouble. They say troops went to arrest two of his entourage on murder charges but they resisted.

Brazzaville emerged from a first night of curfew on Friday. Witnesses reported isolated shots in the city on Friday morning. Soldiers manned roadblocks in the centre of town and restricted movements of vehicles. Most people circulated on foot.
Political parties armed their supporters during ethnic and political fighting which killed 2,000 people following parliamentary elections in 1993.
Last Friday the government banned private militias and the unauthorised carrying of arms, and on Saturday party leaders meeting in Brazzaville pledged to avoid violence.
Clashes between supporters of Sassou Nguesso and former president and prime minister Jacques Joachim Yhombi Opango in their home towns have killed 16 people in less than a month.
Yhombi Opango is Lissouba's campaign manager.

The government said it would pursue two senior members of Sassou Nguesso's guard it held responsible for the clashes. A government statement on Wednesday night also threatened tough measures against anyone carrying an unauthorised weapon.
About a dozen candidates are expected to contest the elections. Frontrunners are Lissouba, Sassou Nguesso and Bernard Kolelas, 1992 runner-up and mayor of Brazzaville.

France has economic interests in the Central African nation and 350 troops there -- left over from an operation to evacuate foreigners from Kinshasa in the last days of the civil war in former Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Brazzaville is just across the river from Kinshasa, capital of the former Zaire.

Sassou Nguesso ran a notionally Marxist single-party administration from 1979 until the advent of multi-party politics in the early 1990s. He then adopted an increasingly pro-Western foreign policy and liberal economic policy.
